what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Founders with leverage should sell shares and lend instead
sections.para: A founder with a profitable, growing product and competing investors can sell existing shares rather than issue new ones, and lend the company growth money as a subordinated loan. Investors get exposure without control, protected instead by open source. The costs are real: lost EIS relief, signalling, a creditor conflict and fine print.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Sell existing shares, lend growth money, keep control
sections.para: The model needs a working product and competing investors. The investor buys the founder's shares, so the company is not diluted and no control changes hands; growth money comes as a subordinated founder loan. Open source is the investor's insurance. Costs include no EIS, signalling and a creditor conflict, and a broad non-compete should be refused.

sections.label: The starting point: a founder who has already won
sections.line: Agents let founders reach profit before raising anything
sections.para: The one precondition is a product with paying customers, profit and growth, and more than one investor wanting in. That used to be rare at seed stage, but agents make execution cheap enough to reach profit first. Then the negotiation flips: the founder does not need the money, the investor needs the deal.

sections.label: Sell, don't issue
sections.line: A founder secondary pays the founder without ceding control
sections.para: The investor buys the founder's ordinary shares in a private sale, so the company is not diluted. Under BADR the first £1 million of gains is taxed at 18% from 6 April 2026, above that 24%. The founder gains security and no board seat is needed; Kaplan and Strömberg found VCs relinquish control when companies perform well.

sections.label: Lend, don't dilute
sections.line: A subordinated founder loan funds growth without new shares
sections.para: If the company needs money, the founder lends part of the sale proceeds back, subordinated to every other creditor, repaid if the company succeeds, at a modest fixed rate or none. The company gets cash without new shares, the founder keeps ownership plus a claim, and no outsider gains control.

sections.label: The open source safety valve
sections.line: Open source replaces control as the investor's insurance
sections.para: If the founder goes rogue, investors can fork the code and fund a better service, since customers stay for service and trust. A fork takes three months at best, realistically a year, to catch up, so it disciplines the founder because it is possible and protects them because it is slow. The licence must be genuinely open.

sections.label: A worked example
sections.line: Selling 20% of £10 million nets about £1.58 million
sections.para: For a £10 million UK company and a £2 million cheque, the founder ends with 80% either way. Selling 20% of their shares, the founder pays about £420,000 tax and keeps about £1.58 million; lending £0.75 million back leaves about £0.83 million. The buyer pays 0.5% stamp duty.

sections.label: Why it could raise the odds
sections.line: Lending their own money makes founders spend carefully
sections.para: Three reasons it could raise the odds: discipline, since Startup Genome found 74% of high-growth internet startups fail from premature scaling; focus, since a founder with money is not tempted by the first acquisition offer; and direction, since the founder keeps the vision without an investor able to force a faster exit.

sections.label: What breaks
sections.line: Lost EIS relief, signalling and creditor conflict are costs
sections.para: UK angels lose EIS and SEIS relief on bought shares. Ordinary shares may be discounted, and Balderton would not expect founders to sell over 10% at growth stage. A founder lender must be subordinated by contract. Transfer rules, HMRC treatment and shareholder agreements matter, and a broad non-compete should be refused.

sections.label: When it works and when it does not
sections.line: It fits profitable, open companies where investors compete
sections.para: The model suits profitable companies growing on revenue, with open code and investors competing. It fits badly for deep tech, hardware, land grabs, EIS-dependent angels, proprietary code or investors insisting on non-competes. A hybrid issues some EIS-eligible shares, sells fewer founder shares and fills gaps with a subordinated loan.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: An untested best case, not tax or legal advice
sections.para: The model assumes leverage most founders lack, and no study tests it; the odds claim and the fork as insurance are arguments. UK figures are for 2026/27, the worked example is illustrative, and the secondary pricing data is thin. The author is a founder running on open source, so has a stake.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: UK tax guidance, VC writing and research
sections.para: The piece comes from a voice memo of 16 October 2026. Sources include gov.uk and HMRC manuals on BADR and EIS, Deloitte, Balderton, Angel Backed, EY India, a German ruling on shareholder loans, Kaplan and Strömberg, Startup Genome, open-source.sgit.ai, NVCA and BVCA model documents and non-compete reviews.
